hero.alt: SST Activities: Explain, Connect Evidence, Apply Ideas. Three numbered steps — a speech bubble with a pencil, documents under a magnifying glass, and a lightbulb pointing toward a mountain path — above a badge reading STAAR to SST.
hero.p1: Classroom activities that build the thinking the Student Success Tool will ask for — explaining, connecting evidence, and applying ideas to new situations — plus a plain-language roadmap of what actually changes when STAAR ends.
hero.p2: Not another stack of test-prep packets. These are short, reusable routines you can drop into instruction you already teach, with teacher look-fors that tell you what to do next.
hero.note: No login. No student data is collected or transmitted. Everything runs in the browser.
sec.sub: Both sets are built for the same thing the draft science blueprints ask for: read a stimulus, use evidence, explain your reasoning. More sets are planned.
card.ace.alt: ACE the SST: Deeper Thinking in Elementary Science. Four elementary students observe a bowl of warm water with a thermometer, beside circles labeled A Articulate, C Connect, E Extend.
card.ace.p: Paired entry and exit tickets built on the ACE framework: Articulate, Connect, Extend. Filter by grade and SST science strand, flip between student and teacher views, and score the response with a SOLO guide that names the next instructional move.
card.words.h2: Break It, Build It — Science Word Parts
card.words.p: Students use Greek and Latin word parts to predict what an unfamiliar science term means, then test that prediction against a diagram, a passage, or data — and revise it when the science disagrees. Twelve printable activities for grades 3–5, in colour and in a black-and-white edition built for a grayscale copier, each with a teacher key.
card.soon.p: Grades 6–8 and 9–12 word-part collections are next, followed by sets for other content areas. Each one follows the same pattern: a short thinking routine, a teacher look-for, and a scoring guide that points to the next move.
road.h2: From STAAR to SST: what actually changes
road.p1: Texas is replacing STAAR with the Student Success Tool. The question most teachers ask first is whether they have to rebuild their course. They do not. What changes is when students are assessed, how quickly results come back, and how much of the reasoning has to be visible.
road.t1: STAAR remains in place through the 2026–2027 school year.
road.t2: Under House Bill 8, SST begins in 2027–2028 with beginning-, middle-, and end-of-year assessments. Grades 3–8 use all three checkpoints.
road.t3: BOY and MOY are optional for the Algebra I, Biology, English I, and U.S. History end-of-course assessments.
road.t4: BOY and MOY are adaptive. EOY is static, so its questions can be released.
road.t5: RLA writing has a separate April window, with other EOY testing in May.
road.t6: TEA says results must reach school systems within two business days after the testing window closes.
road.t7: The English II EOC is eliminated beginning in 2027–2028, though the graduating classes of 2026 and 2027 still have it as a graduation requirement.
road.warnTitle: Read the blueprints without shrinking the curriculum.
road.warnBody: TEA places the same warning on each draft blueprint: all student expectations must still be taught in full. A blueprint identifies the TEKS eligible for the state summative assessment. It is a planning aid, not permission to skip everything that does not fit neatly inside one strand.
road.h3loop: Turn three checkpoints into one teaching loop
road.boyMove: Identify unfinished learning and establish a baseline
road.boyQ: What support does each student need first?
road.moyQ: What changed, and what is still getting in the way?
road.eoyMove: Review mastery, growth, and remaining gaps
road.eoyQ: What should the next teacher know?
road.p2: Your first move is small: bookmark the TEA House Bill 8 page, download the blueprint for your grade or course, and bring one strand to your next planning meeting.
maps.sub: One page per subject, drawn from the draft BOY/MOY and summative blueprints: what is assessed, how many questions, the strand families, and the classroom moves each one rewards. Open an image to see it full size.
maps.sci.alt: SST TEKS map for Science. Assessed: elementary, middle school, Biology, and Spanish elementary science. BOY and MOY hold 22 questions for elementary and middle school and 26 for Biology. Four assessed strands: matter and energy; force, motion, and energy; Earth and space; organisms and environments. Biology extends to structures and processes, genetics, evolution, and environmental systems.
maps.sci.flag: The map behind the activities here
maps.sci.p: Elementary and middle school share four strand families. The summative science blueprints call for stimulus-based clusters, so students need practice interpreting models and data and then using that evidence to explain what is happening.
maps.rla.alt: SST TEKS map for Reading Language Arts. Assessed: grades 3 to 8 and English I, plus Spanish RLA in grades 3 to 5. Two assessed strands, reading and writing. BOY and MOY are adaptive; EOY is static and includes an extended constructed response; RLA writing has a separate April window.
maps.rla.h3: Reading Language Arts: keep reading and writing together
maps.rla.p: Two reporting strands, reading and writing. The summative blueprint adds an extended constructed response, which makes regular evidence-based writing, revision, and editing more useful than a late burst of isolated test practice.
maps.math.alt: SST TEKS map for Mathematics. Assessed: grades 3 to 8 and Algebra I, plus Spanish math in grades 3 to 5. Four assessed strands: numerical representations and relationships; computations and algebraic relationships; geometry and measurement; and data analysis with personal financial literacy. Algebra I adds linear, quadratic, and exponential relationships.
maps.math.p: Four strand families across grades 3–8, with Algebra I adding linear, quadratic, and exponential relationships. Use multiple representations, ask students to explain why a method works, and make error analysis routine.
maps.ss.alt: SST TEKS map for Social Studies. Assessed: grade 8 and U.S. History, sharing four strand families: history; geography and culture; government and citizenship; and economics, science, technology, and society. Grade 8 covers early U.S. history and U.S. History covers 1877 to the present, with source analysis across both.
maps.ss.h3: Social Studies: put sources before summaries
maps.ss.p: Grade 8 and U.S. History use the same four strand families. Students should work regularly with maps, timelines, primary sources, and competing claims. A worksheet of disconnected dates will not build the source analysis these strands demand.
about.h2: How the activities connect to the maps
about.p1: The science map is the one these activities were built against. Its four strand families and its call for stimulus-based clusters point at the same skill: read a model, a data table, or a passage, and use it as evidence for an explanation. Formats change; that skill does not.
about.p2: A student who can only recall a definition stalls the moment a question changes one condition. Both activity sets are designed around that gap, using the same three moves:
about.li1: Articulate — explain what happened in your own words.
about.li2: Connect — tie the evidence to the underlying concept.
about.li3: Extend — predict what changes when one condition changes.
about.w1: ACE the SST when the science content is the point — a lesson on the water cycle, forces, food webs. Entry ticket before, exit ticket after, in seven languages.
about.w2: Break It, Build It when the vocabulary is what is blocking students — when they can read the passage but stall on hydrosphere, photosynthesis, geothermal. Printable, colour or black and white.
about.p3: Both score the thinking with the same four-level guide, so a teacher using both sees one progression rather than two vocabularies.
about.warnBody: Nothing here is SST-approved, official SST practice, or a reproduction of an SST item. Every stimulus was written for these activities. The BOY / MOY / EOY progression used across this area is a local instructional approach for SST readiness, not a TEA requirement.
